lessons.title: Making salts
lessons.programRef: Form 4 Chemistry — Salts, the reactivity series, extraction of metals (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use solubility rules to decide how to make a given salt.
Describe the preparation of a soluble salt from an insoluble base, metal or carbonate, from an alkali by titration, and of an insoluble salt by precipitation.
Describe tests for chloride, sulphate and carbonate ions.
reviewNotes: Solubility rules are the standard school summary (CaSO₄ slightly soluble); check the exact list the syllabus uses. Practicals with hot acid and silver/barium/lead compounds are teacher-led; lead and barium compounds are toxic.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Solubility rules
blocks.md:
- **All nitrates** and all salts of **sodium, potassium and ammonium** are soluble.
- **Chlorides** are soluble except **silver chloride** and lead(II) chloride.
- **Sulphates** are soluble except **barium sulphate** and lead(II) sulphate (calcium sulphate is slightly soluble).
- **Carbonates** and **hydroxides** are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium.

The rules decide the method: a soluble salt is made by **crystallisation**, an insoluble salt by **precipitation**.

blocks.caption: Making a soluble salt from an insoluble base, metal or carbonate.
blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows: warm dilute acid, add excess insoluble base, filter off the excess solid, evaporate then cool and crystallise.

blocks.title: Soluble salts
blocks.md:
**From an insoluble base, metal or carbonate**: add the solid in excess to warm dilute acid until no more reacts; filter; heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation; cool; filter and dry the crystals. Example: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O (blue copper(II) sulphate crystals).

**From an alkali** (all soluble): use a **titration** to find the exact volumes, then repeat without the indicator and crystallise. Example: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O.

blocks.title: Insoluble salts and ion tests
blocks.md:
**Precipitation**: mix two solutions that contain the ions: BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2NaCl (white precipitate), Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2KI → PbI₂ + 2KNO₃ (yellow). Filter, wash with distilled water, dry.

**Tests**: **chloride**: add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate: **white precipitate**. **Sulphate**: add dilute HCl then barium chloride: **white precipitate**. **Carbonate**: add dilute acid: **bubbles of CO₂** that turn limewater milky.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Do not evaporate to dryness: the crystals would form a powder and may decompose; stop at the crystallisation point.
- An excess of the insoluble solid is used so that all the acid reacts; the excess is then filtered off.
- You cannot make a soluble salt from an insoluble one by filtering alone.

blocks.title: Plan a preparation
blocks.statement: Describe how to make zinc sulphate crystals from zinc and dilute sulphuric acid.
steps: Add excess zinc to warm dilute sulphuric acid until fizzing stops (Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂), then filter off the unreacted zinc.
Heat the filtrate to the crystallisation point, cool, filter the crystals and dry them.

blocks.title: Choose a method
blocks.statement: Which method makes silver chloride: crystallisation or precipitation? Give the reagents.
steps: Silver chloride is an insoluble chloride, so use precipitation.
Mix silver nitrate solution with sodium chloride solution: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃.

lessons.title: The reactivity series and displacement
lessons.programRef: Form 4 Chemistry — Salts, the reactivity series, extraction of metals (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: List the metals in order of reactivity and describe their reactions with water, steam and dilute acid.
Predict displacement reactions between metals and solutions of metal salts.
Use the series to explain how metals are extracted and why some metals are stored under oil.
reviewNotes: The mnemonic and the positions of Pb and H are the common O Level ones; check whether tin is included. Reactions of K and Na are teacher demonstrations only.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: The series
blocks.md: In order of **decreasing reactivity**: **K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, (C), Zn, Fe, Pb, (H), Cu, Ag, Au**. Mnemonic: *Please Stop Calling Me A Careless Zebra; Instead Try Learning How Copper Saves Gold.* Carbon and hydrogen are non-metals placed for comparison. Reactivity is the tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions.

blocks.caption: The reactivity series with typical reactions.
blocks.alt: A vertical list of metals from potassium at the top to gold at the bottom with notes: the top ones react with cold water, the middle ones with steam or dilute acid, and copper, silver and gold do not react with dilute acid.

blocks.title: Reactions with water and acid
blocks.md: **K, Na, Ca** react with cold water giving hydrogen and a hydroxide: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ and Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but burns in steam. **Mg, Zn, Fe** react with dilute acid giving hydrogen, quickly for Mg, slowly for Fe. **Cu, Ag, Au** do not react with dilute acid or water. Sodium and potassium are stored under oil.

blocks.title: Displacement
blocks.md: A **more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal** from a solution of its salt: Mg + CuSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Cu; Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (an iron nail gets a brown-red copper coat and the blue colour fades); Cu + 2AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag. The same idea explains the **thermite** reaction: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe. No reaction occurs if the added metal is **less** reactive.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Reactivity is not the same as hardness or density.
- A displacement needs the free metal to be **higher** in the series than the metal in the salt.
- Copper does not displace zinc from zinc sulphate.

blocks.title: Will it react?
blocks.statement: Predict whether zinc reacts with copper(II) sulphate solution, and whether copper reacts with zinc sulphate solution.
steps: Zinc is above copper: it displaces copper: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.
Copper is below zinc: no reaction.
blocks.answer: Yes for zinc; no for copper.

blocks.title: Put in order
blocks.statement: Metal X reacts quickly with dilute acid and displaces Y from Y sulphate; metal Z does not react with acid. Give the order of reactivity.
steps: X displaces Y, so X is more reactive than Y.
Z does not react with acid so it is the least reactive: X > Y > Z.

lessons.title: Extraction of metals and uses
lessons.programRef: Form 4 Chemistry — Salts, the reactivity series, extraction of metals (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain why the method of extraction depends on the position of the metal in the reactivity series.
Describe the extraction of iron in the blast furnace and of aluminium by electrolysis.
State uses of metals and alloys and the value of recycling.
reviewNotes: Industrial processes are simplified; check whether the syllabus requires the electrode equations for aluminium. Cameroon context (bauxite deposits and the aluminium smelter at Edéa) is deliberately not stated as a fact in the lesson; add it only after confirmation.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Ores and extraction
blocks.md: An **ore** is a rock containing enough of a metal compound to be worth extracting. The method depends on reactivity: metals **below carbon** (Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu) are obtained by **reducing the oxide with carbon or carbon monoxide**; metals **above carbon** (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) are too reactive and are extracted by **electrolysis of the molten compound**; unreactive metals such as **gold** are found **native** (uncombined).

blocks.caption: The blast furnace for iron (simplified).
blocks.alt: A furnace with iron ore, coke and limestone going in at the top, hot air entering near the bottom, waste gases leaving near the top, and molten iron and slag leaving at the bottom.

blocks.title: Iron in the blast furnace
blocks.md: Coke burns in hot air: C + O₂ → CO₂; then CO₂ + C → 2CO. Carbon monoxide **reduces** the iron(III) oxide: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. **Limestone** decomposes, CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, and removes sand: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (**slag**, which floats on the molten iron). Iron is tapped from the bottom.

blocks.title: Aluminium and uses
blocks.md: Aluminium is extracted by **electrolysis of aluminium oxide** (from **bauxite**) dissolved in molten **cryolite**, which lowers the working temperature; aluminium forms at the **negative** electrode. It needs a lot of electricity. **Uses**: aluminium (low density, does not corrode because of a thin oxide layer: aircraft, cans, cables); steel (iron with a little carbon: buildings, vehicles); copper (wires, pipes: good conductor); zinc (galvanising). **Recycling** saves ore and energy and reduces waste.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Carbon cannot extract aluminium because aluminium is more reactive than carbon.
- Iron is **reduced** (it loses oxygen); carbon monoxide is **oxidised**.
- Aluminium does not corrode quickly although it is reactive: its oxide layer protects it.

blocks.title: Mass of iron
blocks.statement: Iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃ (relative formula mass 160), contains 2 × 56 = 112 of iron. How much iron could be obtained from 1000 kg of pure Fe₂O₃?

blocks.title: Choose the method
blocks.statement: State the method of extraction for (a) lead and (b) magnesium and explain.
steps: Lead is below carbon in the series: heat its oxide with carbon.
Magnesium is above carbon: electrolysis of the molten compound.
